A Latin name, from Latin Antōnius (Wiktionary).
A Latin name, from Latin patricia “noble”; later also seen as the feminine form of the saint's name Patrick (Wiktionary); borne by 3 women on Roman inscriptions (Epigraphic Database Heidelberg).
A Latin name, from Paulus (Wiktionary); borne by 48 men on Roman inscriptions (Epigraphic Database Heidelberg).
A Latin name, from Latin Antōnius, name of a Roman gens (with excrescent -h- suggested by an unetymological association with Ancient Greek ἄνθος “flower”) (Wiktionary).
A Latin name, from Late Latin saint's name Laura, from the feminine form of laurus “laurel tree” (Wiktionary); borne by 1 woman on Roman inscriptions (Epigraphic Database Heidelberg).
A Latin name, from Latin Iūlia, feminine form of the Roman gens name Iūlius (Wiktionary); borne by 867 women on Roman inscriptions (Epigraphic Database Heidelberg).
A Latin name, from Middle English Mark, from the Latin praenomen (i.e. first name) Mārcus, derived from Mārs, the Roman god of war, originally Māvors, from Proto-Italic *Māwortis (Wiktionary).

A Latin name, from Latin Amanda, feminine form of the saint's name, from amandus, future passive participle of amāre “to love”: thus meaning "who/which is to be loved" (Wiktionary); borne by 12 women on Roman inscriptions (Epigraphic Database Heidelberg).
A Latin name, from Middle English Patrick, from Latin Patricius “patrician”, the name of an early Irish saint (Wiktionary).
A Latin name, from Latin Aemilia. English form of Latin Aemilia, a gens name from aemulus “rival, emulator” (Wiktionary).
A Latin name, from Latin Olīva, an early saints’ name from olīva “olive; olive branch” (Wiktionary).
A Latin name, from Latin Victōria, from victōria “victory” (Wiktionary); borne by 53 women on Roman inscriptions (Epigraphic Database Heidelberg).
A Latin name, from Francia + iscus (Wiktionary).
A Latin name, from Latin natale “birthday (of the Lord)”, referring to birth on Christmas Day, name of an early martyr (Wiktionary).
A Latin name, from Latin Sebastiānus (Wiktionary); borne by 1 man on Roman inscriptions (Epigraphic Database Heidelberg).

A Latin name, from iūstus “just, fair, righteous” + -īnus, from Proto-Italic *jowestos “just, lawful”, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂yew- “upright; justice, law” (Wiktionary); written Iūstīnus in Latin; borne by 90 men on Roman inscriptions (Epigraphic Database Heidelberg).
A Latin name, from Antōnia, the women's form of the Roman name Antōnius; borne by 128 women on Roman inscriptions (Epigraphic Database Heidelberg).
A Latin name, from Paula, the women's form of the Roman name Paulus; borne by 32 women on Roman inscriptions (Epigraphic Database Heidelberg).
A Latin name, from Claudia, the women's form of the Roman name Claudius (Wiktionary); borne by 303 women on Roman inscriptions (Epigraphic Database Heidelberg).
A Latin name, from Virginia, the women's form of the Roman name Virginius (Wiktionary); borne by 1 woman on Roman inscriptions (Epigraphic Database Heidelberg).
A Latin name, from Latin Marius. Italian and Spanish Mario, both of which coming from Latin Marius (Wiktionary).

A Latin name, from Lūcia, the women's form of the Roman name Lūcius; Lūcius is from Old Latin Loucios, from Proto-Italic *Loukjos, related to lūx “light”, stem lūc- (Wiktionary); borne by 29 women on Roman inscriptions (Epigraphic Database Heidelberg).
A Latin name, from Mārcia, the women's form of the Roman name Mārcius; Mārcius is from Mārcus + -ius (Wiktionary); borne by 123 women on Roman inscriptions (Epigraphic Database Heidelberg).
A Latin name, from French Vincent, from Latin Vincentius, from vincēns “conquering”, from the verb vincō (Wiktionary).

A Latin name, from Renāta, the women's form of the Roman name Renātus; Renātus: use as a proper name of the adjective renātus “reborn” (Wiktionary); borne by 4 women on Roman inscriptions (Epigraphic Database Heidelberg).
A Latin name, from Middle English Juliana, from Latin Iūliāna (Wiktionary); borne by 31 women on Roman inscriptions (Epigraphic Database Heidelberg).
A Latin name, borrowed from French Marcel, from Latin Marcellus, diminutive of Marcus (Wiktionary).

A Latin name, from Latin clāra, feminine of clārus “bright, shining, clear”, a post-classical name made famous by the 13th century Saint Clara (Clare) of Assisi (Wiktionary); borne by 5 women on Roman inscriptions (Epigraphic Database Heidelberg).
A Latin name, from Latin Aemilia (Wiktionary).
A Latin name, from Iūlius + -ānus (Wiktionary); written Iūliānus in Latin; a Roman surname (cognomen); borne by 278 men on Roman inscriptions (Epigraphic Database Heidelberg).
A Latin name, from leō “lion” (Wiktionary); borne by 35 men on Roman inscriptions (Epigraphic Database Heidelberg).
of, belonging to a deity, divine

A Latin name, borrowed from Late Latin Diāna, short form of Latin Dīāna, derived by syncope from Old Latin Dīvāna, equivalent to dīvus “of, belonging to a deity, divine” + -āna; roughly akin to Proto-Italic *deiwā “goddess” + Proto-Indo-European *-néh₂ (Lewis & Short).
A Latin name, from Latin Claudius, Claudia (Wiktionary).
A Latin name, from Latin gloria “glory”, first used as a name in 19th-century literature (Wiktionary); borne by 1 woman on Roman inscriptions (Epigraphic Database Heidelberg).
A Latin name, from Rōma “Rome” + -ānus “-an” (Wiktionary); written Rōmānus in Latin; a name of early saints; borne by 87 men on Roman inscriptions (Epigraphic Database Heidelberg).
A Latin name, from Spanish Pablo from Latin Paulus (Wiktionary).
A Latin name, from Latin rēgīna “queen” (Wiktionary); borne by 10 women on Roman inscriptions (Epigraphic Database Heidelberg).
A Latin name, from Latin Fabius; Latin Fabius is from faba “bean” + -ius (Wiktionary).
A Latin name, from Latin Diāna. An anglicization of French Diane, from Latin Diāna (Wiktionary).
A Latin name, from French Valérie, from Latin Valeria; Latin Valeria is from earlier Valesia, from valeō “to be healthy, strong” (Wiktionary).
A Latin name, from Latin Veronīca. Late variant of Berenīcē, influenced by vera icon (Wiktionary).

A Latin name, from French Florence, from Latin Flōrentia (as a given name, a feminine form of Flōrentius), from flōrens “flowering, flourishing”, from flōs “flower”, connected with English bloom and blossom (Wiktionary).
A Latin name, from Latin Beatricem, accusative of Beatrix (Wiktionary).
A Latin name, from French Marc, from Latin Marcus (Wiktionary); borne by 3,315 men on Roman inscriptions (Epigraphic Database Heidelberg).
A Latin name, from Latin laetitia. Name of an early Spanish saint, from Latin laetitia “gladness” (Wiktionary).
A Latin name, from Middle English Austin, from Aostin, Austin, similar to Old French Aostin, Austin, a popular variant of Old French Agustin, from Latin Augustīnus, from Augustus (Wiktionary).
A Latin name, from the French form of the Late Latin saint's name Natalia, from nātālis (diēs) “birthday [of Christ], Christmas” (Wiktionary).
A Latin name, from Latin Claudius (Wiktionary).
A Latin name, from Middle English Maurice, from Late Latin Mauritius, derived from Maurus “Moor; dark, swarthy” (Wiktionary).

A Latin name. Wiktionary on its origin: Name of an early virgin martyr venerated in the Orthodox Church, Latin Marīna, probably a feminine form of Marīnus, from marīnus “of the sea”, or a variant of Marīa; borne by 17 women on Roman inscriptions (Epigraphic Database Heidelberg).
A Latin name, borrowed from French Nathalie, from Latin Natalia (Wiktionary).
A Latin name, from Marco Polo, from Latin Marcus Paulus, from Marcus (Wiktionary).
A Latin name, from Latin silva. Feminine form of Silvius, from Latin silva “forest” (Wiktionary).
A Latin name, from Paulīna, the women's form of the Roman name Paulīnus; Paulīnus is from Paulus + -īnus (Wiktionary); borne by 36 women on Roman inscriptions (Epigraphic Database Heidelberg).
A Latin name, from Latin Laurentius (Wiktionary).
A Latin name, from Latin Clara, with transparent meaning in modern French (claire) (Wiktionary).

A Latin name, from Valentīna, the women's form of the Roman name Valentīnus; Valentīnus is from Valentia + -īnus “-ine” (Wiktionary); a name of early saints; borne by 137 women on Roman inscriptions (Epigraphic Database Heidelberg).
A Latin name, from Latin Lucianus (Wiktionary).
A Latin name, from Latin Vincentius, from vincēns; Latin Vincentius is from vincēns “conquering” + -ius, present participle of vincō (Wiktionary).
A Latin name, from French Émilie, from Latin Aemilia (Wiktionary).
A Latin name, from Latin Beāta. Feminine form of beātus “blessed” (Wiktionary); a name of early saints.
A Latin name, from French Pauline, in turn from Latin Paulīna; in regular use since the 19th century (Wiktionary).
A Latin name, from fēlīx “lucky, happy” (Wiktionary); a Roman surname (cognomen); a name of early saints; borne by 410 men on Roman inscriptions (Epigraphic Database Heidelberg).
A Latin name, from *mārtcus, from the name of the god Mārs + -cus (Wiktionary); a Roman first name (praenomen); borne by 3,315 men on Roman inscriptions (Epigraphic Database Heidelberg).

A Latin name. Wiktionary on its origin: Either 1) from the Latin Beatrix, name of early Christian saints, from beatrix “she who makes happy”, or 2) from beata, influenced by viatrix (“female wayfarer, traveller”).
A Latin name, from Latin norma. Sometimes explained as Latin norma “pattern, model”, or as a feminine form of Norman (Wiktionary).

A Latin name, from Middle English Lucy, from Old French Lucie (notably after the Christian martyr Lucia of Syracuse), from Latin Lucia (feminine of Lucius, a Roman praenomen), from lux “light” (Wiktionary).
A Latin name. Wiktionary on its origin: Derived from Latin silva (forest).
A Latin name. Wiktionary on its origin: from Latin Caelia, feminine of Roman family name Caelius, probably from caelum “heaven”.
A Latin name, from victōria “victory” (Lewis & Short).
Paschal; of or pertaining to Easter

A Latin name, from Latin Paschālis, from paschālis “Paschal; of or pertaining to Easter”, from pascha “Easter” + -ālis, for birth on Easter, or in honor of the 9th-century pope Paschal I (died 824) (Wiktionary).

A Latin name, from Valeria, the women's form of the Roman name Valerius; Valerius is from earlier Valesios, from valeō “to be healthy, strong” (Wiktionary); borne by 432 women on Roman inscriptions (Epigraphic Database Heidelberg).
A Latin name. Wiktionary on its origin: From Latin Caecilia, feminine form of Caecilius, a Roman family name possibly derived from the byname caecus “blind”.
A Latin name, from Latin Hadriānus, Adriānus (Wiktionary).
A Latin name, from Old French Lorenz, from Latin Laurentius (Wiktionary).

A Latin name. Wiktionary on its origin: From the Oscan praenomen 𐌌𐌀𐌓𐌉𐌖𐌔, likely ultimately of Sabine origin and from, originating in Rome; a Roman family name (nomen gentile); borne by 175 men on Roman inscriptions (Epigraphic Database Heidelberg).
A Latin name, from Latin Curtenus. Variant of Courtenay, an aristocratic Norman surname derived from place names in Normandy, from Latin Curtenus, a personal name from curtus “short” (Wiktionary).
A Latin name, from Latin Mārtīna; borne by 19 women on Roman inscriptions (Epigraphic Database Heidelberg).

A Latin name. Wiktionary on its origin: Early saints' name from Latin Vīviānus, and of its feminine form Vīviāna, probably from vīvus “alive”; borne by 7 men on Roman inscriptions (Epigraphic Database Heidelberg).
A Latin name, from Latin silva. Feminine form of a Medieval form of Silvius, from Latin silva “forest” (Wiktionary).
A Latin name, from Latin Vīnicius. Possibly from vīnum “wine” (Wiktionary); a Roman family name (nomen gentile); borne by 23 men on Roman inscriptions (Epigraphic Database Heidelberg).

A Latin name, from Valentia + -īnus “-ine” (Wiktionary); written Valentīnus in Latin; a Roman first name (praenomen) and a Roman surname (cognomen); a name of early saints; borne by 198 men on Roman inscriptions (Epigraphic Database Heidelberg).
A Latin name, from Latin Aurōra. See aurōra “the dawn, daybreak, morning” (Lewis & Short); borne by 1 woman on Roman inscriptions (Epigraphic Database Heidelberg).
A Latin name, from stēlla “star” (Wiktionary); a Roman surname (cognomen).
A Latin name, from Latin Flavius, name of a plebeian Roman gens (Wiktionary).
A Latin name. Wiktionary on its origin: Popular saints' name in the Eastern Orthodox Church, feminine of Latin Tatiānus, from Tatius (a Roman family name of obscure origin) + -ānus.
A Latin name. Wiktionary on its origin: From the name of a third century Roman martyr, Latin Laurentius, "a person from Laurentum", the place name possibly derived from laurus “laurel”.
A Latin name, from Late Latin Dominicus, derived from Dominus “Lord” (Wiktionary).
A Latin name, from Latin Magnus. See magnus “great, large, vast, extensive, spacious” (Lewis & Short); borne by 80 men on Roman inscriptions (Epigraphic Database Heidelberg).
A Latin name, from Silvana, from Latin Silvāna (Wiktionary); borne by 10 women on Roman inscriptions (Epigraphic Database Heidelberg).
A Latin name, from Flāvia, the women's form of the Roman name Flāvius; borne by 317 women on Roman inscriptions (Epigraphic Database Heidelberg).
A Latin name, from Latin Desiderius, from desiderium “desire, longing” (Wiktionary).
A Latin name, from French Laurie, from Latin Laurum, from laurus “laurel” (Wiktionary).
A Latin name. Wiktionary on its origin: From the name of a Roman gens, Latin Aemilius, from aemulus “rival”, or possibly of Etruscan origin.
A Latin name, from Middle English lune, luna “the moon”, from Latin lūna/Lūna, from Proto-Indo-European *lówksneh₂ (Wiktionary).
A Latin name, from Salvador, chiefly various placenames honoring Jesus Christ, from salvador “savior”, from Latin salvator, from salvāre “to save” + -tor (Wiktionary).
A Latin name, from Flōriānus (Wiktionary); borne by 25 men on Roman inscriptions (Epigraphic Database Heidelberg).
A Latin name, from French Cécile, from Cecile, from Latin Caecilia (Wiktionary).
A Latin name, from Latin Mārcus (Wiktionary).
A Latin name, from Late Latin Clēmens (genitive Clēmentis), name of early saints and popes, from clēmens “merciful” (Wiktionary).
A Latin name, from Latin Maurus., which was inherited (Wiktionary).
A Latin name, borrowed from Latin Antōnīna, feminine form of Antōnīnus, derivative of Antōnius (Wiktionary); borne by 2 women on Roman inscriptions (Epigraphic Database Heidelberg).
A Latin name, from Līvia, the women's form of the Roman name Līvius (Wiktionary); borne by 19 women on Roman inscriptions (Epigraphic Database Heidelberg).
A Latin name, from Latin Patricius (Wiktionary).
A Latin name, from Old French; the name of a third century French martyr, from Latin Quīntīnus, a derivative of the Roman praenomen Quīntus, from quīntus “fifth” (Wiktionary).
A Latin name, from Latin amābilis “lovable” (Wiktionary).
A Latin name, from Latin Severinus (Wiktionary).
A Latin name, from French Justine, from Latin Iūstīna, name of early saints, feminine of Iūstīnus, derivative of Iūstus, from iūstus “just” (Wiktionary).
A Latin name, from Latin Didacus. The Portuguese equivalent of Spanish Diego, from Diago, from Latin Didacus (Wiktionary).
A Latin name, from Latin prīscus. Feminine diminutive form of a Roman cognomen Prīscus, from Latin prīscus “former, ancient, old-fashioned” (Wiktionary).
A Latin name, from Latin Augustus; Latin Augustus is from augustus “majestic, venerable”, originally a word of religious use, which was given as a title to the emperor Augustus (Wiktionary).

A Latin name, from Latin Sabīna. Name of early saints, Latin Sabīna, feminine of the Roman cognomen Sabīnus “a Sabine”, from an ancient tribe from Italy (Wiktionary); borne by 110 women and 1 man on Roman inscriptions (Epigraphic Database Heidelberg).
A Latin name, from Latin viola “violet” (Wiktionary); borne by 1 woman on Roman inscriptions (Epigraphic Database Heidelberg).
A Latin name, from Latin mirandus. coined by William Shakespeare for a character in The Tempest; feminine of Latin mirandus “admirable” (Wiktionary).
A Latin name, from French Rosalie, from the Latin saints’ name Rosālia, from rosa “rose” (Wiktionary).
A Latin name, from Latin Celsus, from celsus “high; elevated; noble” (Wiktionary).
A Latin name, from French Céleste, ultimately from Latin caelestis “heavenly” (Wiktionary).
A Latin name, from Latin Flōra (Wiktionary); borne by 32 women on Roman inscriptions (Epigraphic Database Heidelberg).
A Latin name, from French Léonie, from Latin Leonia, feminine of Leonius, derived from leo “lion” (Wiktionary).
A Latin name, from Latin Antōnius (Wiktionary).

A Latin name, from Pia, the women's form of the Roman name Pius; Pius: substantivization of pius “pious” (Wiktionary); a name of the early Church; borne by 22 women on Roman inscriptions (Epigraphic Database Heidelberg).

A Latin name, from Middle English Felicia, from Latin Fēlīcia, from fēlīcia, the neuter plural of fēlīx, which often occurred in the phrase tempora fēlīcia “happy times” (Wiktionary); borne by 8 women on Roman inscriptions (Epigraphic Database Heidelberg).
A Latin name, from Latin Caecilius, a Roman family name derived from caecus “blind” (Wiktionary).
A Latin name, from Latin Iūliānus;, from an borrowing (Wiktionary).

A Latin name, from Augustus; Latin Augustus is from augustus “majestic, venerable”, originally a word of religious use, which was given as a title to the emperor Augustus (Wiktionary); borne by 21 men on Roman inscriptions (Epigraphic Database Heidelberg).
A Latin name, from Maren, from Latin Marina (Wiktionary).
A Latin name, from Latin Mariānus, derivative of the Roman gens name Marius, ultimately from the war god Mars (Wiktionary).
A Latin name, from Latin Aemiliānus (Wiktionary).

A Latin name, from Latin Maximiliānus. Ultimately derived from Maximus + -illus, likely via Maximillus + -iānus, or alternatively, derived from an unattested *Maximilius + -ānus (Wiktionary); a Roman surname (cognomen); borne by 2 men on Roman inscriptions (Epigraphic Database Heidelberg).

A Latin name, from Aurēlia, the women's form of the Roman name Aurēlius; Aurēlius is from aureus “golden” + -lus + -ius (Wiktionary); borne by 754 women on Roman inscriptions (Epigraphic Database Heidelberg).
A Latin name, from Latin Sabinus (Wiktionary).
A Latin name, from Latin Augustus; Latin Augustus is from augustus “majestic, venerable”, originally a word of religious use, which was given as a title to the emperor Augustus (Wiktionary).
A Latin name, from Latin Lūcius; Latin Lūcius is from Old Latin Loucios, from Proto-Italic *Loukjos, related to lūx “light”, stem lūc- (Wiktionary).
A Latin name, from the name of an early Christian saint, Latin serena “serene” (Wiktionary); borne by 16 women on Roman inscriptions (Epigraphic Database Heidelberg).
A Latin name, from Flōrentia; Latin Flōrentia is from flōrens “flowering” + -ia (Wiktionary).
A Latin name, from Fēlīx; Latin Fēlīx is from fēlīx “lucky, happy” (Wiktionary).
A Latin name, from Latin Mārcella. Feminine form of Mārcellus (Wiktionary); a Roman surname (cognomen).
A Latin name, borrowed from Latin lilia, plural of lilium “lily”, or a Latinization of the English Lily (Wiktionary).
A Latin name. Wiktionary on its origin: From Middle English Vyrgyle, from Latin Virgilius, from the Roman clan name Vergilius, from Etruscan and of unknown meaning.

A Latin name, from Latin ara. Shortened from María (de) Araceli, a Roman Catholic epithet of the Virgin Mary as the patron of Lucena, Andalusia, also the name of church in Rome (Madonna di Araceli), from Latin ara “altar” + coeli “of heaven” (Wiktionary).
A Latin name, from Latin vernus. Coined in the 19th century, from Latin vernus “spring-like” or as a feminine of Vernon (Wiktionary).
A Latin name, from Latin Salvātōrem “savior” (Wiktionary).

A Latin name, from Cassia, the women's form of the Roman name Cassius; Cassius: nominative singular deriving from the gens Cassia, a Roman family of antiquity (Wiktionary); borne by 91 women on Roman inscriptions (Epigraphic Database Heidelberg).
A Latin name, from ursa “she-bear” + -ulus (Wiktionary); borne by 41 women on Roman inscriptions (Epigraphic Database Heidelberg).
A Latin name, from Latin Rosālia (Wiktionary).
A Latin name. Wiktionary on its origin: Most likely from Spanish Graciela, ultimately from Latin grātia.
A Latin name, from Latin Renata (Wiktionary).

A Latin name, from Catia, the women's form of the Roman name Catius; Catius is from catus “clear-sighted, intelligent, sagacious, wise” (Wiktionary); borne by 12 women on Roman inscriptions (Epigraphic Database Heidelberg).
A Latin name, from Latin rēx “king” (Wiktionary); borne by 4 men on Roman inscriptions (Epigraphic Database Heidelberg).
A Latin name, from Cornēlia, the women's form of the Roman name Cornēlius (Wiktionary); borne by 148 women on Roman inscriptions (Epigraphic Database Heidelberg).
A Latin name, from Latin Valentīnus, a patronymic from Valēns, itself nominalized from vālens “strong, healthy” + -īnus “-ine” (Wiktionary).
A Latin name, from Latin Augustīnus, derivative of Augustus (Wiktionary).
A Latin name, from Latin clēmentīnus, from Late Latin Clēmens “Clement” (genitive Clēmentis) + -īnus “of or pertaining to”, from clēmens “merciful” (Wiktionary).
A Latin name, from Latin Augusta, feminine of Augustus (Wiktionary); borne by 16 women on Roman inscriptions (Epigraphic Database Heidelberg).
A Latin name. Wiktionary on its origin: From Latin Horatius, a Roman family name of obscure origin, possibly from Etruscan.
A Latin name, from Latin Mārcellīnus, diminutive of Mārcellus, in turn a diminutive of Mārcus (Wiktionary).
A Latin name, from Latin Aurēliō; borne by 1 man on Roman inscriptions (Epigraphic Database Heidelberg).
A Latin name, from Latin benedictus. Based on, Late Latin Benedictus, from benedictus “blessed; well spoken of”, from Latin benedicō. Cf. benito “Benedictine monk” (Wiktionary).
A Latin name, from Octāvius; Latin Octāvius is from octāvus “eighth” + -ius (Wiktionary).
A Latin name, from Latin Cornēlius. Possibly related to cornū “horn” (Wiktionary); a Roman family name (nomen gentile); borne by 484 men on Roman inscriptions (Epigraphic Database Heidelberg).

A Latin name, from Latin clara. Medieval English vernacular form of Clara, from the Latin clara, feminine of clarus “bright, shining, clear”, a post-classical name made famous by the 13th century Saint Clara of Assisi (Wiktionary).
A Latin name, from Latin Facundus. Facundo and Facunda stem from the Latin proper names Facundus/Facunda, from fācundus “eloquent” (Wiktionary).
A Latin name, from maximus (Wiktionary); a Roman surname (cognomen); borne by 675 men on Roman inscriptions (Epigraphic Database Heidelberg).
A Latin name, from Antōnius + -īnus (Wiktionary); written Antōnīnus in Latin; borne by 74 men on Roman inscriptions (Epigraphic Database Heidelberg).
A Latin name, from Italian Giulietta, diminutive of Giulia, from Latin Iūlia, feminine of Iūlius, a Roman family name (Wiktionary).
A Latin name, from the Italian surname, from a personal name derived from Latin laurus “a bay-tree, laurel-tree, laurel” (Lewis & Short).
A Latin name, from the feminine form of the Latin adjective aureus “golden” (Wiktionary).
A Latin name, from French Éloi, from Medieval Latin Eligius, chiefly after Saint Eligius, from Latin ēligere “to pick, to choose from” + -ius “-y: forming adjectives and names” (Wiktionary).
A Latin name, from French Éloy or Éloi, a proper name which is a popular French variant of Latin Eligius, whence also; Latin Ēligius is from ēligō + -ius (Lewis & Short).
A Latin name, from Iustīna (Wiktionary); borne by 48 women on Roman inscriptions (Epigraphic Database Heidelberg).
A Latin name, from rūfus “red, ruddy” (Wiktionary); a Roman surname (cognomen); borne by 432 men on Roman inscriptions (Epigraphic Database Heidelberg).
A Latin name. Wiktionary on its origin: from Latin Lavinia, of obscure meaning.
A Latin name, from Latin Adria, Hadria (Wiktionary).

A Latin name, from Latin Martialis “Roman cognomen”, from martiālis “belonging or dedicated to the Mars, the Roman god of war, or to war”, from Mārs “the god Mars; the planet Mars” + -ālis (Wiktionary).
A Latin name, from Latin Paulus (Wiktionary).
A Latin name, from Latin Hilarius “cheerful, happy”, name of a fourth-century saint, and from its feminine form Hilaria (Wiktionary).
A Latin name, from Latin lux. A modern nonstandard spelling of Lucy, from Lucia, from the Latin feminine form of the Latin praenomen Lucius, from lux “light” "light" (Lewis & Short).

A Latin name, from Latin Catō. According to De Vaan, from Proto-Italic *katō, related to catus “intelligent” with individualizing suffix -ō (< PIE *-e/on-, the "Στράβων" suffix) (Wiktionary); a Roman surname (cognomen); borne by 12 men on Roman inscriptions (Epigraphic Database Heidelberg).
A Latin name, from Januarius “devoted to Janus” (Wiktionary).
A Latin name, from a derivative of Latin silva “wood” (Wiktionary).
A Latin name, from Latin Faustus, a Roman cognomen, and name of early Christian saints, from faustus “happy” (Wiktionary).

A Latin name, from Spanish Cándida,Candida, from Latin Candida, from candida, feminine of candidus “shining white” (Wiktionary); borne by 45 women on Roman inscriptions (Epigraphic Database Heidelberg).

A Latin name, from Latin Albina (name of a third-century martyr), feminine form of the Roman cognomen Albīnus, derivative of Latin albus “white” (Wiktionary); borne by 6 women on Roman inscriptions (Epigraphic Database Heidelberg).
A Latin name, from Alba Longa + -ānus (Wiktionary); written Albānus in Latin; borne by 53 men on Roman inscriptions (Epigraphic Database Heidelberg).
A Latin name, from Latin Fidēlis, name of various saints (see Saint Fidelis), from the fidēlis “faithful” (Wiktionary).
A Latin name, from the noun felicity, and also the English form of Latin Felicitas, a name borne by early martyrs; Latin Fēlīcitās is from fēlīcitās “happiness” (Wiktionary).
A Latin name, from Latin Paulus (Wiktionary).

A Latin name, from Rōmāna, the women's form of the Roman name Rōmānus; Rōmānus is from Rōma “Rome” + -ānus “-an” (Wiktionary); a name of early saints; borne by 30 women on Roman inscriptions (Epigraphic Database Heidelberg).

A Latin name, from Latin Octāvia. Feminine form of the Roman gens name Octāvius, from octavus “the eighth” (Wiktionary); a Roman family name (nomen gentile); borne by 67 women on Roman inscriptions (Epigraphic Database Heidelberg).
A Latin name, from Latin Clēmentem (Wiktionary).

A Latin name, from Latin Titus. Compare 𐌕𐌉𐌕𐌏, Umbrian 𐌕𐌉𐌕𐌉𐌔, 𐌕𐌉𐌕𐌞𐌌. The name was attributed to the Sabines by the ancient author Julius Paris, which may connect to the legendary Sabine king Titus Tatius (Wiktionary); a Roman first name (praenomen); borne by 1,631 men on Roman inscriptions (Epigraphic Database Heidelberg).
A Latin name, from, from Latin Mauritius, from the 3rd-century Egyptian Saint (Wiktionary).
